data.title: Thousand-year-old hillforts of the Slavs – from Vogastisburg to stone castles
data.excerpt: Across the whole of the vast territory they occupied, the Slavic tribes built their fortified seats on elevated ground, where inaccessible terrain offered natural protection; in flat country they relied on watercourses and marshy or lakeside surroundings. Tatiana Štefanovičová follows the Slavic hillforts of the territory of present-day Slovakia from the 7th-century mention of Vogastisburg to the first residential stone towers of the 13th century.
data.metaDescription: How the Slavic tribes built their fortified seats: hilltops, rivers and marshes as natural defences, from the 7th century to the first stone castles.

keyFacts.label: Subject
keyFacts.value: The chronological development of Slavic hillforts in the territory of present-day Slovakia from the 7th to the 13th century

keyFacts.label: Key source
keyFacts.value: The Chronicle of Fredegar – the mention of Vogastisburg and Samo’s Empire (AD 623)

timeline.title: The revolt against the Avars
timeline.description: The Chronicle of Fredegar records a revolt of the Slavs against the Avars, at whose head stood the Frankish merchant Samo – Samo’s Empire came into being, and a victorious battle at Vogastisburg is mentioned.

timeline.title: The hillfort at Mužla-Čenkov
timeline.description: In the last decade of the 8th century, shortly after the demise of the Avar Khaganate, a new hillfort arose on the bank of the Danube near Štúrovo.

timeline.title: The Bavarian Geographer
timeline.description: An anonymous strategic description of the Slavic lands and their strongholds, drawn up for the needs of the Frankish Empire, confirms that fortified seats were characteristic of the Slavic tribes.

timeline.title: Pobedim and other lowland fortified settlements
timeline.description: The well-excavated hillfort of Pobedim near Piešťany comes into being, as does the hillfort of Nitra – Martinský vrch on the northern edge of the former Avar Khaganate.

timeline.title: The union of the principalities
timeline.description: The Moravian and the Nitra principalities are joined into the entity later called Great Moravia, a process accompanied by the rise of central hillforts.

timeline.title: The testimony of Gardīzī
timeline.description: An Arabic source describes the building of strongholds among the Slavs as an inevitable response to Hungarian raids.

timeline.title: The Slovak Gate
timeline.description: A system of hillforts on both sides of the Hron gorge (from Starý Tekov to Hronský Beňadik) is founded or renewed as protection against the advancing Hungarian tribes.

timeline.title: Stone castle architecture
timeline.description: A residential stone tower is built at Bratislava Castle – the beginning of the transformation of timber-and-earth hillforts into masonry stone fortresses.

children.text: When building their fortified seats, the Slavic tribes, across the whole of the vast territory they occupied, most often made use of elevated places, where inaccessible terrain gave them natural protection. In flat country they used watercourses or marshy and lakeside surroundings as natural protection. The protection that nature afforded them they reinforced still further by building fortifications, which often had very ingenious constructions.

Fortified seats – hillforts, which in functional terms were the predecessors of the later medieval castles – are encountered throughout the territory of Slavic settlement. Among the Eastern and Western Slavs this form of settlement is very pronounced, which is why the period in which the Slavic tribes were crystallising is also called the hillfort period, in German terminology Burgwallzeit. Among the Southern Slavs we also encounter Slavic fortified settlements, but there their occurrence is not so pronounced, because they often build upon the fortifications of classical civilisation, which the Slavs frequently captured during their advance into the Balkans and then used for themselves.
The revolt against the Avars

Written sources also inform us about the custom of the Slavs of building strongholds. Among the oldest mentions is the record in the Chronicle of Fredegar. It comes from an unknown annalist who lived at the court of the Frankish-Merovingian ruler Dagobert. He recorded the events connected with the revolt of the Slavs against the Avars in 623, when the Frankish merchant Samo placed himself at the head of the Slavs and the conditions were thus created for the rise of Samo’s Empire. During the fighting of Samo’s Slavs against the Frankish Dagobert, the chronicler states that a serious military encounter, successful for the Slavs, took place at a place called Vogastisburg. We do not know exactly where this place lay – the scholarly literature gives as many as five possibilities – but it was within the territory of Samo’s Empire, which extended somewhere north of the middle Danube. From the ending of the name, burg, we may assume that it was a stronghold. This means that Slavic strongholds – hillforts – were already arising north of the middle Danube in the 7th century, which has recently been confirmed by archaeological excavation as well, especially in Bohemia.

That the building of strongholds was commonplace in the 9th century is told us by another source, the so-called Bavarian Geographer. It is an anonymous description of the lands and strongholds on the northern side of the Danube, drawn up for strategic reasons for the needs of the Frankish Empire in about 815–817. It describes the Slavic tribes and their strongholds in the territory of present-day Germany, Poland, Bohemia, Moravia and Slovakia, but also among the Southern and in part the Eastern Slavs. It states, for example, that “…in Bohemia there are 15 strongholds, the Moravians have 11 strongholds”, and in a later transcript as many as 30 strongholds are given for the Moravians, “…the land of the Bulgars is extensive and has a numerous people and 5 strongholds…” and so on. It cannot be ruled out that with the growing distance of the informant from the particular land the information may be less accurate; it is certain, however, that fortified seats were characteristic of the Slavic tribes and represented a certain potential of power and military force. This emerges quite clearly in an Arabic source of the 10th century (Gardīzī), which states that the building of strongholds is a law among the Slavs: “From all quarters many come together and build strongholds, because the Hungarians often invade them and raid them. The Hungarians defeat them in battle and the Slavs flee into the strongholds they have built”. The source quoted describes the specific situation after the arrival of the Hungarians in east-central Europe. The building of strongholds in the preceding period, however, probably had related reasons, whether it was protection against an enemy from outside, or also the mutual struggles of the individual Slavic tribes among themselves.

In the territory of present-day Slovakia the oldest fortified seats so far attested by archaeological excavation date from the period of the end of the 8th and the beginning of the 9th century. It seems that at the end of the 8th and the beginning of the 9th century a certain process of crystallisation of the individual tribes and efforts at their unification took place in this territory, which was reflected also in the building of fortified seats on which princely retinues settled. Among the well-excavated hillforts of the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries is Pobedim near Piešťany, which by its position in the Váh floodplain ranks among the lowland fortified settlements. In building it the inhabitants of the time made use of a slight rise between the courses of the Dudváh and the Dubová brook, and so there arose a hillfort with a fortified bailey which, according to the observations of the researcher Darina Bialeková, had an unusual construction in some parts of its defences. It consisted of chambers with walls of woven wattle, filled with clay and fired, which produced a kind of fired clay. The chamber with brick walls was then filled with earth. In some parts of the defences the front face of the rampart was formed by a stone wall. Life at the hillfort came to an end sometime in the first half of the 9th century, for graves were sunk into the evidently no longer functional defences in the second half of the 9th century. Despite the demise of the hillfort, the surrounding unfortified hamlets survived throughout the 9th century.
The union of the principalities

Among the important hillforts of this period was Nitra – Martinský vrch, on the northern edge of the Avar Khaganate. Somewhat further south, on the edge of present-day Nitra, there was an Avar cemetery in the 8th century. The results of the excavation of the hillfort are known only from fragmentary information, but it may be assumed that it was one of the important hillforts at which life continued even after the demise of the Avar Khaganate and at the time when Great Moravia was taking shape. This is attested by the find of a single-nave church on its summit. Slavic occupation in the northern peripheral part of the Avar Khaganate must have been intensive and vigorous, for shortly after its demise, in the last decade of the 8th century, a hillfort arose on the bank of the Danube at Mužla-Čenkov, not far from Štúrovo, in surroundings previously settled by the Avars. Another hillfort, as finds mostly from private collectors indicate, probably stood at the beginning of the 9th century at Smolenice. It has not yet been excavated, and so we do not know its character in more detail.

In the northern and eastern parts of present-day Slovakia, too, hillforts arose as early as the beginning of the 9th century as the seats of magnates. In the Orava region it was the hillfort on Ostrá Skala near Vyšný Kubín, in the Spiš region the one in the cadastral area of Čingov. Their fates, too, were not the same. On Ostrá Skala life continued throughout the 9th century; the hillfort at Čingov came to an end around the middle of the 9th century and in its place, not far away, in the cadastral area of Spišské Tomášovce, a new hillfort was built. A similar development took place near Piešťany, where after the demise of the hillfort at Pobedim a fortified seat with a small church – a rotunda – and a manorial court arose on the other side of the Váh, on an older prehistoric hillfort at Kostelisko above the village of Ducové. It was certainly the seat of a magnate and therefore took over the leading role in the middle Váh region.

In the first half of the 9th century a process of unification of the Slavic tribes took place, which at a higher level found expression above all in the joining of the Moravian and the Nitra principalities into the entity later called Great Moravia. This process took place at lower levels as well, and its expression is the rise of more important hillforts with a central function, which had certain more extensive territories under their political and sometimes also ecclesiastical administration.

Among the centres of administrative, political and also ecclesiastical power Nitra undoubtedly belonged, as the most important site of the development of that time, originally the seat of Prince Pribina, later of further princes of the Mojmír dynasty and also the seat of the church organisation. Its importance is underlined by the occurrence of several hillforts within the narrow area of present-day Nitra. Besides the already mentioned hillfort on Martinský vrch, there was the hillfort Na vŕšku, fortified with a massive timber-and-earth rampart, on the site of which the church and monastery of the Piarists were later built. An important role was also played by the hillfort on the site of the later bishop’s castle, where a bishopric was probably located already in the time of Great Moravia. Views of this hillfort were long sceptical with regard to its Great Moravian history, because no corresponding finds of the period came from it. This was caused, however, by the extensive medieval and modern built-up character of the whole area and the impossibility of carrying out excavation on it. Only in recent years, when excavation was undertaken, did it become clear that the medieval castle had been founded on an older Slavic hillfort, which probably ranked among the most important in Nitra.

Another hillfort with a central political and also ecclesiastical function was undoubtedly Bratislava Castle, fortified with a massive timber-and-earth rampart, which had a smaller stone palace building on its summit and, lying further to the east of it, a three-nave stone church with walls decorated with painting, which had graves of the 9th century around it. Both sites, Nitra and Bratislava, retained their importance later as well, in the period of the emerging Kingdom of Hungary, when they became its comitatus castles.
The function of Devín

Some hillforts of the 9th century also became the centres of comitati. Excavation, however, has not demonstrated such a pronounced function of central administration here. These are Starý Tekov and Zemplín. By coincidence, a later medieval and modern cemetery lay over their area, which made their investigation impossible. It therefore cannot be ruled out that important older finds may still lie hidden on them. A central function in the 9th century may also have been held by strongholds which did not later have to become comitatus castles of the Kingdom of Hungary; in the lower Hron region, for example, Bíňa certainly had an important function. Its fortification is, it is true, dated only to the 10th–11th century, but the graves of a smaller cemetery in its central part, not far from the later Romanesque rotunda, date from the 9th century and, by their rich furnishings, are attributed to the leading stratum of the society of that time.

The function of the stronghold of Devín, which is among the best-known hillforts connected with the history of Great Moravia in Slovakia, cannot be interpreted entirely unambiguously. The church with a trefoil apse uncovered by archaeological excavation on the lower summit part of the hillfort suggests the seat of a magnate. Alongside Bratislava, however, probably not one of central importance. It is certain that the whole area of Devín and Bratislava was protected by further smaller guard hillforts. At the foot of Devínska Kobyla there were two hillforts of the 9th century – Na pieskoch and Lom. From the eastern side the territory could have been protected by the hillfort Nad Neštichom near Svätý Jur, originally considered to be later, from the end of the 9th and the beginning of the 10th century. Newer finds, however, attest to its existence already at the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries.
Fear of raids

The building of strongholds is very characteristic of the 9th century. Some sites in central Slovakia have also been well investigated by excavation. Among the important fortified seats was certainly Vyšehrad, between the Turiec Basin and the Upper Nitra region, which could also have had the function of a central stronghold for one of the areas mentioned. In the Zvolen Basin it was the hillfort of Môťová near Zvolen, but the hillfort in the cadastral area of the village of Detva was important as well. In eastern Slovakia, besides Zemplín, the important hillforts were above all Šarišské Sokolovce, whose development reaches further into the 11th century and which by their area belong among the extensive fortifications. In the Spiš region, besides the already mentioned hillforts at Čingov and Spišské Tomášovce, there was also a hillfort on the hill of Dreveník, at the eastern end of which Spiš Castle was later built. The hillfort lay at the opposite end, above Spišské Vlachy, and would deserve the attention of research.

At the end of the 9th and the beginning of the 10th century hillforts were founded or re-fortified as protection against the advancing Hungarian tribes. Among them is the system of hillforts in the so-called Slovak Gate, on both sides of the Hron gorge, from Starý Tekov in the south as far as Hronský Svätý Beňadik with the hillfort on Beňadická skala in the north. Between them lie three further hillforts, which together protected against penetration northwards through the Hron gorge.

The character of the fortified settlements – hillforts – remained unchanged in the following period as well. The hillforts had a considerable area, divided into a main part – the acropolis – and outer settlements, which mostly adjoined it in a ring.

Even in the 12th century the defences consisted mostly of repaired or also new ramparts of timber-and-earth construction with a possible stone front wall. A marked change came only at the end of the 12th century and in the first half of the 13th century, when under the influence of western castle architecture stone architecture arose in the territory of present-day Slovakia as well. At first it took the form above all of residential stone towers, such as those that arose at Bratislava Castle in 1245, or at Trenčín, perhaps somewhat earlier, as well as at Spiš Castle and others. Later stone palace buildings were added to them, and then masonry defences as well, and the castles took on the appearance of stone fortresses as we know them today.
Tatiana Štefanovičová
